newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Turkey vows to slash budget deficit.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Turkey vows to slash budget deficit.

text.p: Turkey's new government, preaching both reform and innovation, told investors on Monday it aimed to reduce a budget deficit that analysts fear is reaching crisis proportions by slashing state borrowing by the end of next year.
At mid-year Turkish finance minister Abdullatif Sener said the country's public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) would be equivalent to around 10 percent of gross national product.
But analysts in London say it is already approaching 13 percent -- a level higher than that reached in the months before Turkey slipped into economic crisis late in 1993.

"Our government's first objective it to reduce the PSBR and if possible to get rid of it altogther," Sabri Tekir, Turkish state minister and member of the government's economic council, told Reuters in an interview in London.
"I think we will be able to reduce the PSBR by the end of 1997 by a significant level," he said.
"In order to achieve this we are going to use fiscal policies and monetary measures, but our major instrument will be to use our own resources and attract foreign investors to invest in Turkey."
Tekir was in London to outline the thrust of his two-month old government's economic policy to London financiers.

But foreign investors are sceptical. They want to see real commitment to privatisation, and fear Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's move last July, granting a higher-than-expected public sector wage rise of 50 percent, means populism rather than economic orthodoxy is order of the day.
Describing his Welfare party as one of "reform and innovation", Tekir said changes to the country's tax collecting procedures was a priority, to be implemented ideally in the first half of 1997.
"We want to regulate the unofficial economy," he said.
He said the country was planning to cut the highest tax level from 55 percent to 40 percent, and the lowest band, currently at 27 percent, would be reduced to 10 or 15 percent.
Early payment would be rewarded with reduced liabilities.
But he conceded that economic conditions for Turkish businesses were tough.

"We're now living in a high inflationary period and are suffering from high real interest rates," he said. "We have to deal with these problems...we have to reduce the PSBR because it is putting a heavy burden our our economic system."

Turkish inflation is running at dizzyingly high levels, with the wholesale price index set to increase by 90 percent this year. Interest rates are also touching prohibitive heights -- currently around the 40 percent mark.
An unwieldy official trade balance of some $20 billion this year, not made any more manageable by an appreciating lira, is also worrying investors, despite the size of Turkey's informal economy.
Tekir said Turkey was working towards a trade balance in the second half of 1997, and was aiming at single digit inflation, though he declined to give a timeframe.

He denied Turkey was lukewarm on privatisation, despite setback after setback over the past decade. This time round his Welfare party saw no parliamentary barriers to staste sell-offs, and Turkish Telecom would spearhead the process soon, he said.
Chemical company Petkim would be next on the blocks and a number of state utilities were set to follow, he added.
He said he government would prove investor-friendly, and would provide the political stability that investors crave but which has eluded the country for much of this year.
"I can assure you our government will not have a short life," he said.
